stages.title: Data: pretrain and mid-train
stages.tagline: Raw code, cleaned and mixed. Where a model learns what code looks like.
stages.who: Most useful if you train from scratch or continue pretraining. If you only have a few GPUs, you will mostly use this stage to borrow a filtered subset or to understand what your base model already saw.
decide: Continue pretraining a good open base model, or start from scratch. For almost everyone the first option wins on cost: a strong open code base model already carries most of the signal.
How much to filter. Quality filters (educational or textbook-style classifiers, license filters, deduplication) usually pay back more than adding raw volume.
Whether to add a short high-quality annealing or mid-training phase (synthetic, reasoning-heavy, repo-level data) at the end of pretraining.
pitfalls: Near-duplicate files inflate benchmark scores and waste tokens. Deduplicate at file and repository level before you train.
Benchmark contamination: remove problems and solutions from your eval sets from the training mix, then confirm with a held-out or post-cutoff eval.
Licenses are per file. A corpus being open to download does not mean every file in it is permissively licensed. Read the card and keep the license metadata.

stages.title: SFT: instructions, reasoning, trajectories
stages.tagline: Teach the format: follow instructions, explain, edit, call tools, solve step by step.
stages.who: The first thing most teams run on an existing base model. Cheap, fast to iterate, and the stage where data quality is most visible in the numbers.
decide: Instruction data versus reasoning traces versus agent trajectories. Pick by the goal: short answers and edits need instructions; competitive programming benefits from long reasoning traces; repository tasks need multi-turn trajectories.
Teacher model and license: synthetic datasets inherit the terms of the model that wrote them. Check each card.
How much data. Several published recipes get strong results with a few tens of thousands of carefully filtered examples, so start small and measure.
pitfalls: Training on data generated from the benchmark's own problems (or paraphrases) gives inflated scores and a model that is no better in practice.
Unverified synthetic code often contains wrong solutions. Execute it or test it, and drop what fails.
Mixing too many styles can degrade formatting. Keep a chat template and a loss mask on responses only, and check outputs by eye.

stages.title: Preference and reward data
stages.tagline: Teach what better means: pairs and judgments that rank code, ideally grounded in tests.
stages.who: Useful when SFT has plateaued and you want a cheap alignment step before (or instead of) full RL. Pairs derived from test results are far more reliable than pairs judged by another model alone.
decide: Execution-grounded pairs (passes tests versus fails tests) versus LLM-judged pairs. Prefer the first where you can get it.
Whether to train a reward model or skip it. For code, tests are often a better reward than a learned model, so verifiable-reward RL can replace this stage.
DPO versus other offline methods. Use the simplest one your trainer supports and compare on a held-out eval.
pitfalls: LLM-judged preferences reward style and length. Control for length, or your model learns to write longer code.
Pairs where both samples pass (or both fail) carry little signal. Filter to pairs with a clear outcome gap.
Preference data built from a benchmark's tests can leak that benchmark into training.

stages.title: RL with verifiable rewards
stages.tagline: Let the model try, run the tests, reward what passes. Environments, task sets, and verifiers.
stages.who: For teams that can afford many rollouts and have a trustworthy verifier. It is the stage that most often moves hard-reasoning and agentic scores, and the stage where mistakes in the verifier become reward hacking.
decide: Which task source: unit-tested function problems, competitive programming with test cases, repository issues with containerized tests, terminal tasks, SQL with execution match, or formal proofs checked by a proof assistant.
Which filter on difficulty. Tasks the model always solves or never solves give no learning signal, so keep a middle band of pass rates.
Which framework runs the rollouts and where the sandbox lives.
pitfalls: Reward hacking: models edit or special-case tests, read hidden tests from disk, or use the network when it is on. Isolate the sandbox and keep tests out of reach.
Weak or sparse tests reward wrong code. Add test cases, or check them with a reference solution before using a task.
Run RL after the model already solves a fair share of tasks. From a weak start, most rollouts fail and the signal is thin.

stages.title: Evaluation
stages.tagline: Benchmarks and harnesses. How you know whether anything worked.
stages.who: Everyone. Run a small fixed set of evals before you change anything and after every stage. Prefer evals that refresh or are hard to contaminate, and keep one private set of your own.
decide: A fast smoke test (minutes) and a slower gate (hours) so you can iterate without waiting on the expensive one.
At least one execution-based eval that matches your goal: function-level, repository-level, terminal, or SQL.
How to report: pass@1 with a fixed sampling setup, the number of samples, and the seed or a confidence interval.
pitfalls: Saturated or contaminated benchmarks make every model look good. Track a time-sliced or private eval next to the classic ones.
Different harnesses give different scores for the same model. Pin the harness version and prompt format, and compare like with like.
Some benchmark instances have flawed tests or ambiguous statements. Read failures by hand before you trust a small difference.

stages.title: Tools: data pipelines, sandboxes, trainers
stages.tagline: Dedup, decontamination, sandboxes, and the frameworks that run the training.
stages.who: The supporting cast. Pick tools by what you already run: a single GPU box, an HPC cluster with Apptainer, or a managed cloud.
decide: Data tooling: how you deduplicate, decontaminate, filter licenses, and remove personal data.
Sandbox: Docker with strict flags on one machine, rootless containers on a cluster, or a hosted sandbox service.
Trainer: a simple SFT trainer first, an RL framework only when you are ready for rollouts.
pitfalls: Running model-generated code on your host. Always use a container or VM with no network and limited memory, CPU, and processes.
Rolling your own dedup or decontamination without testing it on known duplicates.
Choosing an RL framework before you have a verifier. The verifier is the hard part.
